> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

text.text: Modern models of preferential decision making have achieved substantial success in predicting choice behaviour both qualitatively and quantitatively, but often overlook related aspects such as response time or confidence.

In parallel, recently proposed mental sampling frameworks have offered broad explanations for multiple aspects of behaviour including probability judgments, perceptual estimates and numerical forecasts, but have not yet been applied to preferential choice.

Here, we seek to unite these lines of research by extending one such framework, the Autocorrelated Bayesian Sampler (ABS; Zhu et al., 2024), to decisions between alternatives which differ in the value of their potential outcomes.
text.formatted: Here, we seek to unite these lines of research by extending one such framework, the Autocorrelated Bayesian Sampler (ABS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Zhu et al., 2024)</ref>, to decisions between alternatives which differ in the value of their potential outcomes.

text.text: We present a new version of the ABS adapted to such decisions, the Autocorrelated Bayesian Decision Maker (ABDM), able to predict not just choices, but also reaction times and confidence in selections.
We compare the predictions of the ABDM against extant choice and response time data in risky choice tasks, finding strong correspondence in both.
We also contrast the new model against leading explanations for behaviour in such tasks, showing the ABDM is competitive in choice and ahead in response times.
We thus propose this model as a broader approach to decision making capable of explaining multiple measures from a common process.
The Autocorrelated Bayesian Decision Maker: Mental Sampling Processes Capture Preference, Confidence and Response Time in Risky Choice

We often must make decisions between alternatives where an objectively superior option is difficult to define or entirely absent: for example, which meal to order at an unfamiliar restaurant, whether a new phone's features are worth the price, or whether a new medication will cure a symptom.
Determining how we make choices in such scenarios is thus of vital importance both to deepen our understanding of human behaviour as well as to help guide people toward better decisions.
Naturally, then, many potential theories have been offered to capture how people make such choices, with almost 100 decision making models proposed over the last 70 years (He et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Naturally, then, many potential theories have been offered to capture how people make such choices, with almost 100 decision making models proposed over the last 70 years <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(He et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In many cases, these theories have been designed to accommodate observed behavioural patterns which violate earlier models: expected utility theory offers reasons for violations of expected value via subjective transformations of value (Bernoulli, 1954), prospect theory offers reasons for violations of expected utility via reweighting of probabilities (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979), cumulative prospect theory offers reasons for violations of prospect theory via distinct accumulation processes for gains and losses (Tversky & Kahneman, 1992), and so on.
text.formatted: In many cases, these theories have been designed to accommodate observed behavioural patterns which violate earlier models: expected utility theory offers reasons for violations of expected value via subjective transformations of value <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bernoulli, 1954)</ref>, prospect theory offers reasons for violations of expected utility via reweighting of probabilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Kahneman & Tversky, 1979)</ref>, cumulative prospect theory offers reasons for violations of prospect theory via distinct accumulation processes for gains and losses <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Tversky & Kahneman, 1992)</ref>, and so on.

text.text: The result of this has been a series of models steadily improving in their ability to capture choice behaviour, both in terms of reducing quantitative error between predicted and empirical choice rates and matching qualitative choice phenomena (Bhatia, 2014; Birnbaum, 2008; Erev et al., 2017; Kellen et al., 2020).

text.text: This is particularly evident in recent models leveraging machine learning techniques to provide high predictive accuracy in large-scale data (Peterson et al., 2021; Plonsky et al., 2025).

text.text: At the same time, the overarching focus on choice within these models has arguably led to a deep but possibly narrow understanding of decision making: modern models certainly offer strong performance in predicting choices, but predictions of related aspects such as decision confidence or time are rarer, while others such as estimates and valuations of prospects are often entirely distinct.

Such a focus is perhaps understandable given that choices are ultimately the main consequential aspect of decision making, but these other responses can themselves offer insight into the choice process.

A key example is the time taken to make a decision: more difficult choices often take longer, providing an indication of the time course of the underlying cognitive systems (Ayal & Hochman, 2009; Glöckner & Betsch, 2008).

text.text: Consideration of these measures can thus offer a more complete understanding of choice behaviour via the relations between choice and other response types, which risks being overlooked in models strictly focused on predicting selections.
A contrasting approach to this line of work is to attempt to provide a more general model of behaviour which includes decision making as one of the many actions a person can take.
This principle underlies the Autocorrelated Bayesian Sampler (ABS), a general purpose cognitive framework that can be applied to a wide range of potential tasks (Zhu et al., 2024).

text.text: The ABS proposes that much of behaviour may be based on a consistent underlying mental sampling process in which agents repeatedly simulate possible cases in their mind and use these simulations to guide responses: for example, when faced with a simple perceptual stimulus like a field of dots, people may iteratively imagine a series of potential counts of the actual number.

This set of samples can then be used in various ways to answer questions on the original stimulus: the mean of the samples provides an estimate of the target value, the relative proportion of samples above or below a boundary value (e.g., higher vs. lower than 25) can act as a judgment of the probability of that classification, and the number of samples needed to make a classification can predict the response time.
Importantly, this means that samples collected for one query can be reused for another, creating links between responses which may be missed by narrower models focusing on one response at a time.

This trades on the flexibility of mental sampling as a cognitive process: simulated samples offer rich sources of information able to answer multiple queries from a common source, while the generality of sampling allows for applications to a broad range of domains.

The ABS draws upon a series of recent studies offering sampling-based explanations for observed behaviours in varying tasks, including perceptual decisions, probability judgments and numerical estimates (Dasgupta et al., 2017; Lieder, Griffiths, Huys, et al., 2018; Spicer et al., 2022 Spicer et al., , 2024;; Zhu et al., 2020).

text.text: The findings of this work inform the specific sampling algorithm at the core of the ABS: for example, samples are assumed to be autocorrelated due to common violations of independence in human response series (Castillo et al., 2024; Castillo et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2022), and samples are moderated by a prior on beliefs to avoid overly polarised judgments when relying on small sample sizes (Sundh et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2020).

text.text: More generally, the ABS uses the consistency of these patterns between tasks to propose a common underlying psychological system supporting varying aspects of behaviour from low-level perception to high-level reasoning.

There is however a key caveat to this model: the ABS uses sampling to approximate the probability of particular responses within an individual's mental distribution, but does not consider how these responses may differ in their value.

This may be sufficient in simple objective cases where the decision maker need only consider the accuracy of their choice (as in the field of dots example above), but may not contend well when the available alternatives offer substantially different rewards: for example, a monetary gamble may have a low probability of paying out, but if the potential win is high enough, it may still be worth playing.
As such, despite the breadth of its framework, the ABS is not well suited to capturing preferential choice in its current implementation.
This is not to say that sampling cannot be applied to such choices: in fact, mental sampling models have become increasingly prominent in recent decision making research.

Key examples include Decision Field Theory which uses sampling to capture the allocation of attention to potential outcomes (Bhatia, 2014; Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993), 'Decision by Sampling' approaches which draw samples from memory to determine the relative rank of an outcome within the decision maker's psychological distribution (Noguchi & Stewart, 2018; Stewart et al., 2006), the Best Estimate and Sampling Tools (BEAST) model which combines biased sampling mechanisms with expected value when evaluating options (Erev et al., 2017), and Utility Weighted Sampling which prioritises sampling of outcomes which would have the greatest impact on the decision maker (Lieder, Griffiths, & Hsu, 2018).

text.text: Much like the ABS, these models assume decisions are driven by mental simulation, in this case generating the potential outcomes of a particular choice in the mind and selecting according to the results of these simulations.
As previously referenced, however, these models principally focus on choices, with little to no consideration of related behaviours such as confidence or valuation.
There thus remains a gulf between even these sampling models of decision making and the broader sampling framework of the ABS, preventing a more unified description of choice behaviour.

In this paper, we seek to bridge this gulf by extending the ABS to preferential choice, connecting the existing framework with established models of value-based decision making to create an even broader depiction of behaviour.

We suggest that such a combination offers benefits for both individual lines of work: expanding the ABS to such choices not only increases the scope of this particular model, but also provides a more general account of decision making, including potential relationships between response types overlooked by existing choice-focused models.
In the following sections, we first introduce the current sampling framework of the ABS, then describe how this can be extended to preferential choice scenarios.
We then assess the adequacy of this model by comparing its predictions to available data, as well as contrasting its performance with other leading models of decision making.

Crucially, we examine the model's predictions on multiple response types (choice, response time and confidence) to assess its breadth of coverage, drawing all measures from a single common posterior distribution.
Finally, we close with discussion of the implications of this newly developed model for both theories of preferential choice and sampling approaches to cognition.
The Autocorrelated Bayesian Sampler (ABS) proposes a consistent rational framework underlying a number of human behavioural responses (Zhu et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The Autocorrelated Bayesian Sampler (ABS) proposes a consistent rational framework underlying a number of human behavioural responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Zhu et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The ABS approximates full Bayesian inference via a sequential sampling process in which samples are drawn from an internal psychological distribution over potential hypotheses.

These samples are assumed to be able to answer multiple potential queries, including estimates, probability judgments and basic decisions between alternatives (for example, whether a particular target value is higher or lower than some boundary).
In the case of such decisions, each sample is treated as evidence for one particular selection, with an accumulation process aggregating this evidence as more samples are taken.
This results in a posterior distribution approximating the probability of each choice within the psychological distribution.

We shall first detail the current process of the ABS to provide a foundation for its modification for value-based choices, separating the model into three distinct components for clarity: the sampling space, the autocorrelated sampling algorithm, and the evidence accumulator.
Before beginning sampling, it is first necessary to define the space from which samples will be drawn.

In the existing definition of the ABS, this is a psychological distribution within the mind reflecting the probability of particular states of the world according to that individual's mental representation.

The definition of this distribution is purposefully left open to allow the framework of the ABS to be applicable to multiple potential tasks, scenarios and queries: states could reflect perceptual properties of a given stimulus (e.g., the number of dots on a screen), empirical distributions of particular values (e.g., the ages of a group of people) or inferred beliefs (e.g., the future price of a financial asset).
Similarly, the source of this psychological distribution is deliberately undefined within the ABS as the model is only concerned with how the mental representation is used once it has been acquired.
As its name suggests, a key tenet of the ABS is that samples are not independent of one another but are autocorrelated, with each new sample being related to its predecessors.

For this purpose, the ABS uses a particular sampling algorithm named Metropolis-Coupled Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MC 3 ) in which multiple sampling chains run in parallel, differing in their propensity to explore the psychological distribution.
On each timestep, each chain proposes a new potential sample given its most recent sample, and probabilistically decides whether to accept or reject this proposal.

This can itself be divided into separate subcomponents: the starting point of the sampler, the proposal function determining new values, and the swapping of chains as a distinct exploratory aspect of the MC 3 algorithm.

Because the autocorrelated sampling algorithm proposes similar values to the preceding sample, sequences are inherently biased towards their starting point under a limited number of samples as there is less potential for movement away from this initial value.
As such, the setting of this value can substantially impact the resulting series of samples, and therefore any decisions based on them.
A basic setting for this value is simply to draw an initial random sample from the space, meaning any starting point bias is eliminated across simulations.

One notable alternative to this however is to set the starting point to prominent values offered by the query (for example, a boundary between responses), as in this case the resulting starting point bias offers an explanation for anchoring effects where estimates are drawn towards presented values (Lieder, Griffiths, Huys, et al., 2018; Spicer et al., 2022).
text.formatted: One notable alternative to this however is to set the starting point to prominent values offered by the query (for example, a boundary between responses), as in this case the resulting starting point bias offers an explanation for anchoring effects where estimates are drawn towards presented values <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Lieder, Griffiths, Huys, et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Spicer et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The proposal function generates a new potential sample at each timestep given the most recent sample in that chain.

This uses a Gaussian distribution with the latest sample as its mean: where Y c,t is the proposed value at time t for chain c, X c,t-1 is the most recent sample in that chain, and σ controls the width of the proposal function.
This distribution is then itself sampled to produce a proposal value for that chain, with more similar values thus being more likely to be proposed.

Proposals are then assessed by comparing their probability against that of the preceding sample in that chain using the Metropolis-Hastings rule: where both p(X c,t-1 ) and p(Y c,t ) are the probabilities of those events within the sampling distribution, while p(Y c,t |X c,t-1 ) and p(X c,t-1 |Y c,t ) reflect the proposal probabilities as defined in Equation 1.

As the proposal function here is Gaussian, these two proposal probabilities are equal and so cancel out for the present definition, but we retain these here to aid extension to other cases using non-symmetric proposal functions.

The parameter τ c meanwhile reflects the temperature of chain c, moderating its tendency to move to lower probability regions: higher temperatures make probabilities more even, increasing the likelihood of such moves.
Temperatures are initialised according to: to ensure one chain remains undistorted (i.e., τ1 = 1), with φ controlling the temperature increment between the exploratory chains.
If the proposal is rejected, the previous sample is repeated (i.e., X c,t = X c,t-1 ).
While the multiple chains of MC 3 allow for greater exploration of the sampling space, the sampler ultimately only produces one key sample on each timestep, taken from the undistorted chain.

In order to make use of this explorative ability, the sampler compares the values produced by each chain and probabilistically determines whether to swap their positions using a similar decision rule to that determining sample acceptance above.

After each chain either accepts or rejects its most recent proposal, chains are randomly paired (without replacement) and the probability of these values at their current positions are contrasted with the probability if these positions were exchanged: with swaps being selected according to this probability.
This then allows for larger movements of the undistorted chain where a higher temperature chain discovers a high probability region and these positions are exchanged.
In order to make a choice, samples are converted into evidence towards a potential selection, with an accumulator aggregating this evidence as the sampler progresses.

Samples are thus converted into single units of evidence for the prospect favoured in that sample (e.g., 'higher' or 'lower'), essentially counting the number of 'wins' for that option across the sequence.
This is a purely ordinal comparison with no consideration of magnitude: for example, a sample of 26 dots and a sample of 30 dots are equally supportive of the 'higher than 25' response.

This results in a posterior distribution approximating the probability of each response within the psychological distribution, being either a Beta distribution for binary decisions or a Dirichlet distribution for multialternative decisions: where p(h i |s) is the probability of response i given samples s and the β parameters reflect the counts of samples supporting each of k possible responses.

While the evidence accumulator tracks the output of the sampling algorithm, it is also initialised with a prior to capture pre-existing expectations on the likelihood of each response before sampling begins.

These priors can be viewed as 'pseudocounts' of assumed observations before actual sampling begins, with their relative proportion reflecting pre-existing expectations of the likelihood of each considered response.

This prevents extreme polarization of the evidence accumulator when only a few samples have been taken: for example, after a single sample, all evidence will naturally favour one response, which may lead to overconfidence that this response is correct (Zhu et al., 2020).

text.text: This prior can then be adapted according to experience with the task, for instance favouring a response which has occurred more frequently in past trials.
The stopping rule determines whether sufficient evidence has been accumulated to cease sampling and make a selection.

As the accumulator tracks wins against losses, the stopping rule is defined by a fixed threshold measuring the difference in evidence count between options (or between the top two options in multialternative cases), with this threshold being an additional free parameter of the model.

Despite the relative simplicity of this rule, such a heuristic offers a reasonable approximation of the optimal stopping rule in such decisions (Dragalin et al., 1999 (Dragalin et al., , 2000)), and has been suggested to be used by actual learners (Brown et al., 2009).

text.text: Once sampling is terminated, the decision maker is assumed to select the option with the highest probability in the final posterior distribution.
In addition to this choice, the set of collected samples also predicts both the time taken to reach this decision and confidence in the selection.
Response time is based on the number of samples taken before termination, assuming that each sample carries a time cost to produce.

This is captured using a Poisson process where the delay between samples is exponentially distributed, resulting in an Erlang distribution: where n is the final sample count and λ is number of samples generated per second.
The expected RT is then simply the sample count divided by the sampling rate:

Confidence meanwhile is based on the mean of the final posterior distribution: in both binary and multialternative cases, this is simply the relative proportion of samples (including the prior) supporting the chosen option:

Importantly, this means that these responses are based on the same set of evidence, leading to relationships between response types; for example, more conflicted evidence leads to more even posteriors and hence lower confidence, but also higher sample counts as it is more difficult to meet the termination threshold, resulting in longer RTs.

Decisions in the current ABS are thus based on an approximation of that option's probability within the internal distribution, where higher sample counts provide better approximations but are restricted by the optional stopping rule.

As previously noted, this suffices for basic perceptual or cognitive tasks where the available options carry equivalent values as decisions need only consider the expected accuracy of selecting the most likely alternative.
Such a definition fails however to account for cases in which the available options carry differing values, meaning the ABS is currently unable to effectively simulate preferential choice tasks.
Before attempting to apply the ABS to value-based decision, we should first specify the format of the choices which it must solve as this will determine some aspects of the new definition.

For this purpose, we use the risky choice paradigm in which decision makers must choose between options varying in both monetary outcomes and the probability of receiving those outcomes (e.g. 100% chance of £10 vs. 50% of £20, 50% of £0).

We shall initially focus on scenarios in which both the possible outcomes and their associated probabilities are provided ahead of the choice (so-called 'decisions from description') rather than being learned through observation ('decisions from experience'), though we will return to the influence of experience later.
We shall also focus exclusively on choices between two risky prospects rather than multialternative choice as this is the more common paradigm in previous work.

Such choices have been a focus of extensive work in decision making research, commonly using behavioural patterns in these tasks to identify underlying systems and discriminate between potential decision models (Bhatia, 2014; Birnbaum, 2008; Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993; Erev et al., 2017; Glöckner & Pachur, 2012; Kellen et al., 2020; Tversky & Kahneman, 1992; Zhao et al., 2020).

text.text: In addition, the probabilistic nature of these choices offers a closer match to the existing probabilistic nature of the ABS, allowing for easier application.
Having set the task, we next offer a new definition of the ABS adapted to risky decisions.

We name this the Autocorrelated Bayesian Decision Maker (ABDM) to distinguish this new definition from its predecessor, though we view this as an extension of the same underlying sampling framework rather than an entirely separate model.
The ABDM samples the potential outcomes of an actual choice, with an accumulator tracking the evidence towards each selection as more samples are collected.

This follows the approach of many existing mental sampling models treating samples as mental simulations of possible outcomes (Bhatia, 2014; Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993; Erev et al., 2017; Lieder, Griffiths, & Hsu, 2018).

text.text: Such a change does however require alterations to many of the components of the ABS outlined above, including the addition of new model functions and parameters.
In some cases, these changes are intended to offer greater flexibility in model behaviour, allowing for interpolation between specific model settings rather than static rules.
The following section thus redefines the components of the model, noting any changes from the previous definition.

The parameters of this posterior are determined by two factors of the decision maker: their confidence in the stated probabilities, and their own personal prior on probability.

For the former, this is captured by assuming that the stated probability is itself the mean of the posterior of the person providing the gamble description (again being either a Beta or Dirichlet distribution depending on the number of outcomes): this essentially treats the probabilities as reported proportions from an assumed previous set of samples with total n d , where higher counts imply greater confidence in the listed values (Fennell & Baddeley, 2012).

For simplicity, we assume this prior is uniform across available options, treating all events as equally likely a priori, though the magnitude of this parameter can vary to reflect the strength of this prior: higher β 0 values imply stronger prior beliefs.

For simplicity, we use a common starting rule for all chains within the sampler, meaning each chain in a given simulated choice begins at the same point even under the random rule.

As the sampling space is now divided into discrete events, the proposal function is here defined using a Markov transition matrix where the probability of proposing each event is determined by the similarity between that event and the most recent sample (see Figure 2B).

text.text: We use this matrix in place of the Gaussian proposal from the previous definition (see Equation 1) to prevent the sampler from proposing entirely impossible events with zero probability in the mental distribution.

text.text: To retain a form of autocorrelation in the samples, transition probabilities are set using an exponential function of the squared difference between events, moderated by an additional free parameter h:
Low h values thus produce more uniform proposal distributions, while high h values increase focus on the most similar event.
This setting is also supported by recent findings that people prefer transitions to more similar values when explicitly generating sequences of potential decision outcomes (Spicer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This setting is also supported by recent findings that people prefer transitions to more similar values when explicitly generating sequences of potential decision outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Spicer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: As an additional parameter, we also vary whether proposed repetitions of the latest event (i.e., p(Y c,t = X c,t-1 )) are permitted as these lead to the same sample value whether accepted or rejected; such exact repetitions are almost impossible for continuous scales but become far more probable for discrete events, particularly if transition probabilities are based on similarity as the most similar value to any outcome is naturally itself.

Preventing these proposed repetitions thus increases the efficiency of the sampler, as well as corresponding Illustration of the autocorrelated sampling algorithm of the ABDM: a starting point for the chain is first selected, here being the most probable event (A).
A new potential value is then drawn from the proposal matrix given this value based on similarity in events (B) and compared against its predecessor to determine acceptance (C).
with the apparent aversion to direct repetitions in repeated generations (Castillo et al., 2024; Spicer et al., 2026).

text.text: This is achieved by setting the probability of repetitions to zero and normalising the remaining transition probabilities.
Note that this only prevents repetitions in proposed values: the previous sample can still be repeated if a proposal is rejected.
Proposals are then assessed by comparing their probability against that of the preceding sample in that chain using the Metropolis-Hastings rule as defined in Equation 2.

text.text: For simplicity, samples are again converted into single units of evidence for the prospect with the better outcome in that sample.
This does mean however that evidence is based primarily on the probability of each gamble outperforming the other with no consideration of the degree of difference in value.

As such, we include an additional parameter here determining how often this conversion is performed: rather than converting each individual sample into evidence, conversion instead occurs every n steps using the mean of the last n samples (illustrated in Figure 3), with this count being a free parameter.
text.formatted: As such, we include an additional parameter here determining how often this conversion is performed: rather than converting each individual sample into evidence, conversion instead occurs every n steps using the mean of the last n samples (illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref>), with this count being a free parameter.

text.text: This then allows the ABDM to approximate the expected difference between options, with n controlling the fidelity of this approximation: high ns provide more accurate estimates leading the model to tend towards expected utility, while low ns continue to focus on the probability of advantage as in the original ABS.

As in the previous definition of the ABS, the evidence accumulator is initialised with a Beta prior to capture pre-existing expectations on the likelihood of each response, fitting with the continued accumulation of discrete units of evidence for each choice.
This is initially fixed and uniform across options for all choices to reflect no pre-existing bias, but can be updated as experience with these options is gathered.

As the accumulator continues to track wins vs. losses, the stopping rule is here again defined by a fixed threshold measuring the difference in evidence count between options, with this threshold being an additional free parameter of the model.

For practical purposes, we also include an absolute limit of 1000 total samples to avoid indefinite sampling where evidence is indecisive; if this limit is reached, the model selects the option with the higher win count at that point regardless of the threshold, or selects randomly if counts are equal.
The final set of samples can then be used to direct choice according to the maximum of the posterior distribution as in the ABS.
This also includes predictions of response time based on the final sample count (following Equation 7) and confidence based on the posterior mean (following Equation 8).
text.formatted: This also includes predictions of response time based on the final sample count (following Equation <ref type="formula" target="#formula_7">7</ref>) and confidence based on the posterior mean (following Equation <ref type="formula" target="#formula_9">8</ref>).

text.text: As with many other models, there remains the possibility that the above processes are not perfectly executed, leading to additional noise beyond the stochasticity inherent within the sampling algorithm.
The ABDM includes two sources of such noise: within the accumulator, and when selecting responses.

Accumulator noise reflects errors when converting samples to evidence, captured by adding Gaussian noise to the average over recent samples, with the variance of this Gaussian being a further free parameter: meaning evidence is more likely to be miscalculated where the mean of the sampled values is closer to 0.
Response noise reflects errors when making the final selection such as typing errors, captured by a fixed probability of choosing the alternative gamble to that favoured by the sampler.

Following previous model definitions (Erev et al., 2017), accumulator noise is not included for dominated choices where one option is clearly superior to the other, but response noise is included in these cases as this is independent of actual values.
text.formatted: Following previous model definitions <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Erev et al., 2017)</ref>, accumulator noise is not included for dominated choices where one option is clearly superior to the other, but response noise is included in these cases as this is independent of actual values.

text.text: Thus far, the ABDM has remained focused on purely descriptive scenarios in which all relevant information on the available prospects is provided ahead of choice.
We next consider how the behaviour of this model may change when experiencing the outcomes of previous choices.

Such a distinction is an important consideration given that past work has observed differing behavioural patterns between these domains: for example, decisions from experience suggest underweighting of rare events, in contrast to overweighting of rare events commonly observed in description (Hertwig et al., 2004; Wulff et al., 2018).

We incorporate feedback into the model by treating these observations as additional samples within the evidence accumulator, adding actual outcomes to the simulated counts to further update the posterior with external evidence.
As with mental samples, feedback values can be translated into wins and losses for each alternative, allowing them to be added on top of the counts generated in the mind.
This method will however only reflect the probability of that option outperforming the alternative with no consideration of the degree of difference.

As such, we tune the update from each set of feedback values to reflect the degree of advantage in that observation, relative to the range of outcomes in that choice: where β A,t is the posterior parameter for option A on trial t after sampling is terminated and A t and B t are the respective outcomes of gambles A and B on that trial (an equivalent update is applied to β B,t ).
The minimum feedback value in that trial is also subtracted to prevent negative increments to the distribution parameters.

This updating process is however specific to only that particular pair of options, and resets back to the symmetrical form described above when moving to a new problem to reflect no substantive prior preference.
To evaluate the predictive ability of the new ABDM, we must compare it against current leading theories from the literature.

We therefore selected four competing models to provide a contrast with the ABDM, chosen to reflect key models of decision making proposed in previous work, including existing sequential sampling models.
We next briefly introduce these models before comparing their performance with the ABDM.
'Best Estimate and Sampling Tools' (BEAST) is an alternate sequential sampling model aiming to capture the qualitative choice phenomena in both description and experience (Erev et al., 2017).
text.formatted: 'Best Estimate and Sampling Tools' (BEAST) is an alternate sequential sampling model aiming to capture the qualitative choice phenomena in both description and experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Erev et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In brief, BEAST also offers a sampling explanation for choice behaviour, but with several notable differences from the ABDM: first, BEAST switches between four sampling methods within its sampling process, each reflecting particular behavioural biases (unbiased sampling from the true probabilities, uniform sampling reflecting equal weighting, focus on the lowest available outcome to capture pessimism, and focusing solely on the sign of outcomes).

Selection of these sampling tools is stochastic, with increasing probability of the unbiased tool as more feedback is observed: where t is the number of trials with feedback, β controls the baseline tendency towards the biased sampling tools and θ reflects sensitivity to feedback.
Second, BEAST takes a fixed number of samples in every decision, treating this count as a stable property of the decision maker (denoted κ).

Third, samples are used alongside an approximation of that option's expected value, with the difference in both estimates between alternatives directing choice: where ∆ t is the estimated difference on trial t, BEV is the best estimate of an option's expected value, ST is the mean across samples for that option, and ε is normally distributed noise.

Where all outcomes and their probabilities for an option are known, BEV matches the true expected value (i.e., ∑ i p(x i )x i ); if probabilities are unknown (so-called 'ambiguous' gambles), BEV is instead inferred via a weighted average of a uniform weighting of the outcomes, the expected value of the alternative option, and the minimum outcome: where ψ reflects the decision maker's sensitivity to ambiguity by controlling the weight applied to the lowest outcome min(B).
This allows BEAST to make choices when comparing an ambiguous gamble against an unambiguous alternative, but not between two ambiguous gambles.

Fourth, BEAST resamples for every trial: feedback is instead incorporated into the unbiased sampling tool, using the store of observed outcomes as a source for mental samples in place of the listed probabilities.
As the number of observations grows, proportions within this store will eventually converge to the true probabilities, though greater discrepancies will appear in earlier decisions.
BEAST also increases its likelihood of using the unbiased tool as the amount of feedback increases (see Equation 16), meaning later choices will more closely follow objective probabilities.

text.text: BEAST offers a valuable standard for model evaluation as this provided strong performance in the comparison of Erev et al. (2017), with even the better performing models in that competition using BEAST as a foundation.

text.text: Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT) is a well-established choice model that has been dominant in risky choice for over thirty years (Tversky & Kahneman, 1992).
text.formatted: Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT) is a well-established choice model that has been dominant in risky choice for over thirty years <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Tversky & Kahneman, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike the ABDM and BEAST, CPT is not a sequential sampling model, but instead estimates the values of available options using subjective transformations of both value and probability.
Outcomes are first separated into gains and losses, and ordered by magnitude within each branch.
Subjective value is then determined using distinct utility functions for each domain: where λ is a loss aversion parameter.

Subjective probabilities are calculated for each outcome using a weighting function that considers the difference between the cumulative probability of outcomes as extreme as that outcome and those that are strictly larger: where i, j and k are the ranks of the outcomes. w(p) is the subjective weighting function of probability:
The γ parameter controls the distortion of this function: if γ = 1, weights match probabilities, but where γ < 1, weights are shifted towards more central values.
text.formatted: The γ parameter controls the distortion of this function: if γ = 1, weights match probabilities, but where γ < 1, weights are shifted towards more central values.

text.text: Following the original definition of Tversky and Kahneman (1992), we use distinct weighting parameters for gains and losses, denoted by differing symbols (γ where x ≥ 0, δ where x < 0), though the function remains the same.
text.formatted: Following the original definition of <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Tversky and Kahneman (1992)</ref>, we use distinct weighting parameters for gains and losses, denoted by differing symbols (γ where x ≥ 0, δ where x < 0), though the function remains the same.

text.text: The final valuation is then a combination of the weighted utilities from each domain: where subscript g denotes gains and subscript l denotes losses.
CPT also differs from the sampling models as its estimates are deterministic, meaning preferences are fixed for a particular set of parameters.
To provide a choice probability, estimates are passed to a softmax function: where θ controls sensitivity to the difference in estimated values.
Decision Field Theory (DFT) is also a sequential sampling model, though somewhat simpler than either the ABDM or BEAST.

DFT assumes sampling reflects stochastic allocation of attention to potential outcomes, where the sampling rates are proportional to the probability of those outcomes occurring (Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993).
text.formatted: DFT assumes sampling reflects stochastic allocation of attention to potential outcomes, where the sampling rates are proportional to the probability of those outcomes occurring <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: These samples are then iteratively added to a running estimate of the difference in value between the options: where ∆ t is the estimated difference between options A and B after t samples, x A,t and x B,t are the latest samples, u(x) is a utility function, and ε t is normally distributed noise.
Sampling ends when the estimated difference exceeds some threshold θ, with choice being determined by the sign of the difference.
Like the ABDM, the number of samples needed to meet this threshold also gives an estimate of the response time assuming a particular sampling rate.
Following Bhatia (2014) and Kellen et al. (2020), we use an extended version of DFT in which decision makers are occasionally 'distracted' and attention becomes evenly allocated across outcomes.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bhatia (2014)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Kellen et al. (2020)</ref>, we use an extended version of DFT in which decision makers are occasionally 'distracted' and attention becomes evenly allocated across outcomes.

text.text: This is achieved by a weighted combination of the true probabilities and a uniform distribution across potential outcomes: where q(x i ) is the probability of sampling outcome x i , p(x i ) is that outcome's true probability, n is the number of possible outcomes and π is the probability of distraction.

While analytical solutions for the probability of particular choices in DFT are available (Bhatia, 2014; Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993; Kellen et al., 2020), we here use simulation to provide model predictions to capture the stochasticity of the sampling process, as well as for parity with the ABDM and BEAST which do not hold simple analytical solutions.

text.text: As with the ABDM, we include an absolute limit of 1000 samples to prevent indefinite sampling where evidence is mixed.

The transfer of attention exchange (TAX) model is similar to CPT in that it also produces valuations of each option using subjective weighting and utility functions rather than sequential sampling, though with some key differences (Birnbaum, 2008).

text.text: First, TAX does not separate between gains and losses, ordering all outcomes in a single ranking.
This also means that the utility function is equivalent between domains, with no loss aversion parameter.
Second, the probability weighting function is a power law applied to the true probability:

Third, TAX transfers weight between the possible outcomes, with the direction of transfer depending on an additional parameter δ: where ω(p i , p k , K) is the weight transferred from outcome i to outcome k and n is the total number of outcomes. δ controls the direction and size of transfer: if δ > 0, weight transfers from higher ranks to lower ranks, whereas if δ ≤ 0, weight transfers from lower ranks to higher ranks.

text.text: We next evaluated the predictive ability of the ABDM by fitting the model to empirical data, beginning with choices themselves.
This also includes comparison against the other candidate models to measure the ABDM's relative performance against current leading descriptions of choice behaviour.
We assessed the performance of the candidate models by simulating choices on a set of 150 risky choice problems taken from Erev et al. (2017).

text.text: We use this dataset for model evaluation as it provides empirical choice rates for several major choice phenomena from a common participant sample: 30 of the problems capture prominent behavioural effects observed in previous decision making research, reflecting common criteria for model assessment in this field (Bhatia, 2014; Birnbaum, 2008; Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993; Erev et al., 2017; Kellen et al., 2020; Tversky & Kahneman, 1992).

text.text: The remaining 120 problems meanwhile provide a generalisation to a wider set of choices for a broader perspective of choice behaviour.

Another advantage of this data set is that problems were answered both with and without feedback: each choice is repeated 25 times, with feedback on actual outcomes from each gamble beginning on the sixth trial.
Choice rates are thus separated into five blocks, each collecting five trials, where block 1 represents choices from description alone and subsequent blocks reflect increasing amounts of experience.
This then allows for examination of behaviour in both description and experience, and the transition between.

Model performance was assessed both qualitatively and quantitatively: qualitative fit was measured according to the model's ability to produce the choice phenomena targeted in the gamble set, such as preference for certainty in gains but not losses, aversion to risk and losses, and differences in choice when outcomes are split into separate components.

Each effect is defined by choices between monetary gambles, with model targets being set according to empirical choice rates across participants, either reflecting preferences for particular options, or preference patterns between two related choices.

Effects are thus measured at the aggregate level rather than the individual level based on whether the majority of decision makers select a particular option. 14 total effects are included in the gamble set, with 10 occurring in description and 4 occurring in experience.
Descriptions of these effects are given in Table A1.

text.text: Quantitative fit meanwhile was assessed using numerical measures of the difference between empirical and simulated choice rates.

We use two quantitative fit metrics: first, we examine the mean squared deviation (MSD) between the average choice rate across model simulations and the empirical choice rate across participants, collapsed across problems, matching the metric used by Erev et al. (2017).

(2017)</ref>.

text.text: Second, we calculate the marginal log likelihood (MLL) of the model by determining the probability of each choice made by each participant and averaging across parameters, allowing for individual level fitting.

We use marginal likelihoods as opposed to maximum estimates to control for the size of the parameter space within the likelihood itself, meaning no further adjustments for model complexity are required.

The candidate models were simulated by sampling 100 independent parameter sets from their prior distributions (listed in Appendix B) and using these to predict selections in each of the 150 target problems.

To allow fitting of individual participants, choice probabilities were defined for each problem for a given parameter set; for the sampling models (ABDM, BEAST and DFT), this was done by repeating simulations 100 times and taking the proportion selecting an option as its likelihood, thus reflecting the inherent stochasticity of the sampling algorithm.
This also included response noise described above for these models to prevent likelihoods of 0 where all simulations favoured one option.
For CPT and TAX, this used the softmax function from Equation 23.

text.text: To further support individual-level fitting, we updated the ABDM's predictions using the actual feedback sequence viewed by each participant to capture their exact experience in the task.
BEAST resampled on each trial to allow its increasing use of feedback (see Equation 16).

text.text: CPT, DFT and TAX meanwhile all offer no method to incorporate feedback information and so were only simulated for the first trial of each gamble pair, with subsequent trials assuming the same choice probability.
CPT, DFT and TAX also have no method to account for ambiguous scenarios where explicit probabilities are not given, though in this case these models are completely unable to make predictions.
As such, we assume in these cases that these models predict indifference (i.e., choice probabilities are 0.5).

We use this assumption to maintain equal numbers of empirical observations for each model to aid comparison of likelihoods, though we also examine model performance when excluding ambiguous cases in Appendix C as a robustness check.

Once calculated, these probabilities were compared against each participant's choices to determine likelihoods, which were then aggregated across trials to produce their likelihood at that parameter set and subsequently marginalised across simulations.
Individual-level marginal likelihoods were then logged and summed across participants to produce an overall measure of model performance.

To calculate MSD, we produced posterior predictive choice rates for each participant: individual-level likelihoods were normalised across simulations to produce posterior distributions for each participant, which were then used to weight the predicted choice rates of each simulation to create posterior predictive rates for each individual for each model.
We then averaged these posterior predictive rates across participants to produce group-level predictions.
As in Erev et al. (2017), predicted rates were also averaged in blocks of 5 trials before being compared to equivalent empirical measures.

As previously referenced, however, the ABDM is a broader description of 690 behaviour than many existing choice models, meaning advantages may emerge when considering other response types.
The next section thus expands this comparison to evaluate performance on another aspect of choice behaviour, response time.
As previously noted, a particular advantage of the ABS framework is that it produces multiple response types from a consistent sampling process (Zhu et al., 2024).

text.text: This strength is inherited by the new version of the model: in addition to predicting choice, the ABDM also predicts the time taken to make that choice, as dictated by the number of samples drawn before the accumulator passes its threshold parameter.
This uses the same Erlang distribution of response time given in Equation 6: by assuming a particular sampling rate λ, the ABDM can also simulate RTs alongside predicted choices.

text.text: What is more, this means the ABDM can predict decision times even without directly fitting equivalent empirical data, instead inferring these times directly from choice simulations.
The competing models meanwhile vary in their ability to predict choice response times.
As noted above, DFT also assumes response times reflect the number of samples taken to reach the threshold, meaning this count can be used to estimate RT by assuming a particular sample rate.

A similar process can be applied to BEAST: while this model was not intended to produce response times, as this also assumes a mental sampling process, the sample count can again be used to predict response times under a given sampling rate.
Unlike the ABDM and DFT, however, BEAST assumes this sample count is fixed for all trials and gambles for a particular decision maker, meaning variations can only emerge between individuals.
In contrast, CPT and TAX do not natively offer any predictions of response time, providing only valuations of each option.

As such, to allow these models to compete on this measure, we supplemented them using Drift Diffusion Models (DDMs) translating choice parameters to predicted response times: this converts model valuations into a 'drift' term reflecting the tendency towards a particular selection which can be used to estimate the expected time to reach a threshold for choice (Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008; Ratcliff et al., 2016).

text.text: RT estimates were then derived from these fitted simulations using mixed-model regressions predicting empirical RTs according to model-specific factors reflecting their assumptions on the decision process: for the ABDM, BEAST and DFT, this used the posterior mean number of samples drawn for each problem, meaning the fitted coefficient estimates the time taken to produce each sample.
For CPT and TAX, this used the estimated time from the supplementary DDM, translating the arbitrary units of the diffusion process to meaningful time.

In addition, to capture the time needed to read the available options when first presented, all regressions included the number of joint outcomes in that gamble pair as a predictor, reflecting the complexity of that choice problem; this was assumed to only impact the first trial of each pair, with the count for subsequent trials set to zero.

Regressions also adjusted their predictors according to the assumed time course of each model: as the ABDM assumes sampling only occurs in the first trial for a particular gamble pair, sample count was set to 0 for all subsequent trials.

In contrast, BEAST and DFT assume sample counts are stable across repetitions and so use the same count for all trials, though BEAST also assumes sample count is stable across problems for a given individual.
The DDM estimates used by CPT and TAX were also assumed to be stable across trials but could vary between problems and individuals.
All regressions included random intercepts and slopes for the considered predictors to capture individual differences in pace.

The ABDM thus offers a better description of the time course of decisions than other choice-focused models, even when these are supplemented with additional mechanisms to to decision making: the sampling framework underlying the ABDM offers a wider coverage 791 of behaviours than existing theories, allowing it to capture aspects that others may miss.
We 792 therefore next extend this even further by considering another response modality, confidence.
In addition to predicting the time taken to make a decision, the ABDM also inherits its predecessor's ability to predict the decision maker's confidence in their selection.

This follows the ABDM's use of sampling to approximate the probability that an option is better than its alternative, captured by the posterior distribution produced after sampling is terminated: the final sample counts for each alternative form a Beta distribution whose mean represents the expected probability of advantage (see Equation 8).

text.text: Model evaluation on confidence is also complicated by the fact that the competing models make no formal predictions regarding confidence at all, offering no point of comparison with the ABDM.

Furthermore, unlike the previous comparison of response times, it is difficult to even define a baseline for these models: while we could assume new methods to extract confidence measures from the operation of these models, these would be highly speculative and not reflective of the original definitions of these theories.
This then prevents a direct model comparison of the form used in the previous sections.

As such, rather than directly comparing predicted confidence judgments from each of the candidate models to empirical data, we instead here evaluate the ABDM's predictive ability in confidence by examining particular qualitative patterns in the model's simulations.

This targets three main relationships between confidence and other measures raised by previous research: the relation between confidence and choice, the relation between confidence and RT, and the relation between confidence and the value of the stimuli.

We assess each of these using the posterior predictions on these measures across both datasets from the previous simulations, where the posteriors are again defined at the individual level based only on fits to each participant's choices.

While confidence is always derived the same way from the model, we use two different codings of confidence depending on the comparison: option coding provides the confidence in a given alternative even if that is not what was ultimately selected, while choice coding provides the confidence in the actual selection, creating a lower bound of 0.5.
As choices here are all binary, choice coding is simply the complement of option coding where that alternative was not favoured (i.e., con f (A) = 1con f (B)).
For simplicity, we restrict these analyses to only the first trial of each gamble to focus on the internal samples before incorporating feedback.

These results thus show the ABDM is able to capture key effects in confidence from the decision making literature, further illustrating the breadth of its coverage.
This stands in sharp contrast to the competing models which all offer no predictions of confidence at all.

The above comparisons demonstrate the Autocorrelated Bayesian Decision Maker's ability to describe human decision making, showing that it not only accurately predicts choice behaviour in general terms but is also competitive with other existing leading models, even outperforming some well-established theories.

This correspondence is both quantitative and qualitative: the ABDM demonstrates good numerical fit to empirical data and captures most of the key phenomena observed in choice, again demonstrating an advantage over previous models.

What is more, our results show that the ABDM in fact offers more accurate predictions of the time taken to make such choices than these competitors, thus better explaining the time course of these decisions.
We have also shown the ABDM can describe key qualitative phenomena in confidence, further outperforming its competitors which do not consider this measure.

These results illustrate the breadth of this approach described in the Introduction to this paper: by proposing a detailed sampling process underlying choice, the ABDM provides a more multifaceted depiction of this behaviour, considering how sampled evidence determines not just selections but other related responses like response time and confidence.

This breadth does not end with these responses, however: as with its predecessor, the ABDM is also able to predict valuations of the alternatives as well as confidence intervals around these valuations (Zhu et al., 2024).

Further contrasts with such data are thus a key avenue for future work, particularly where all response types are given from a single task and participant sample to allow for examination of their relations to one another.

This is contrasted with the behaviour of the more specialised models in our comparisons: considering choice alone, BEAST provides the best description, demonstrating the advantage of focusing on one particular aspect of behaviour.

Such an advantage could in fact be even greater for more recent models which use modern machine learning techniques to provide even closer matches to empirical choice rates (Peterson et al., 2021; Plonsky et al., 2025).

text.text: Evaluation of the other response types show where these models can fall down, however: none of the competing models match the ABDM's ability to predict the time course of decisions and offer no predictions of choice confidence, revealing the limitations of their approach.
The ABDM thus provides a better description of behaviour when considering more aspects than just the immediate choice rate, so offering a more 'complete' account.

In fact, a similar argument could be applied to the more specialised models as well: BEAST is itself a broader model than the other candidates, considering the additional influence of feedback and ambiguity on decisions.
From this perspective, the ABDM takes this a step further by expanding not just the set of choice problems that can be modelled, but also the range of responses drawn from these problems.

This is not to suggest that the ABDM completely captures all behaviour in these tasks, of course: as with any computational model, some detail must be lost to make it tractable, inevitably leading to an imperfect description.

At the same time, the ABDM does provide substantially wider coverage of behaviour than other leading models, not only predicting multiple aspects of the choice process, but also linking this to other behaviour in perception and judgment from its prior definition (Zhu et al., 2024).

text.text: The value of this broader approach is not just in providing a more complete theory of behaviour, but also in identifying the practical implications of the processes actually supporting decision making: understanding the underlying cognitive systems reveals the possible interactions between responses which may be missed if focusing purely on choice.

The response time analyses provide a demonstration of this: because RT in the ABDM depends on the number of samples needed to make a choice, this model links RT to the difficulty of a decision, with longer RTs reflecting more conflicted evidence and hence harder choices.

These patterns are however ignored by base CPT and TAX which generate immediate estimates of choice without considering how the difficulty of that comparison might impact its speed (Ayal & Hochman, 2009; Glöckner & Betsch, 2008).
text.formatted: These patterns are however ignored by base CPT and TAX which generate immediate estimates of choice without considering how the difficulty of that comparison might impact its speed <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ayal & Hochman, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Glöckner & Betsch, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: This is not however an inherent trait of process models, also demonstrated by our comparisons: both BEAST and DFT propose sequential sampling processes support choice but fail to fully account for variation in RT.

The reasons for this are more specific to these models: DFT does attempt to predict the time course of decisions but ignores the influence of experience, predicting consistent behaviour across repetitions, while BEAST uses a fixed sample count for a given person, preventing variations in RT across both trials and problems.

Similarly, confidence in the ABDM reflects the relative proportion of samples favouring each choice, meaning more mixed evidence results in more moderate confidence, as well as longer RTs as more samples are needed to meet the threshold.

Identifying these underlying systems also allows for new predictions of likely behaviour where the process is constrained by external factors: for example, adding a time limit to decisions may further restrict the amount of considered evidence, thus strengthening the influence of the starting point and prior on responses and so leading to different decisions.

Our results also indicate that the narrowness of choice-focused models cannot be easily solved by simply appending these models with additional mechanisms: we find that supplementing both CPT and TAX with a Drift Diffusion Model to allow predictions of response time does not lead to a better description of this data.

This is particularly important given such mechanisms have become increasingly common as general purpose explanations for behaviour in this field: DDMs have had substantial success in recent years in matching both the choice and timing patterns of human decision makers in perceptual (Drugowitsch et al., 2012; Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008) and preferential tasks (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich & Rangel, 2011).

text.text: Moreover, DDMs have also been extended to allow for judgments of confidence (Pleskac & Busemeyer, 2010) and continuous valuations (Kvam & Busemeyer, 2020), providing their own form of breadth.

text.text: The present results however suggest that DDMs are not a universal solution for capturing such behaviour, offering little additional explanatory power for the response times observed in the tasks examined here.

This being said, our comparisons consider only a fairly basic form of DDM without starting point bias or variation in parameters across trials; this was a deliberate decision to avoid diverging from the predictions of the base choice models, but may limit the predictive ability of these approaches.
Continued contrasts with DDMs are thus a key avenue for future work.

There are also more theoretical distinctions between DDMs and the form of breadth discussed here: while DDMs are highly versatile, no single setting captures all response types, instead requiring separate diffusion processes for each modality.
As such, while DDMs may capture the relation between a response and its timing, they do not predict direct connections between differing responses such as choices and valuations.

This is in contrast to the use of a consistent sampling process for multiple responses in the ABS, leading to relations between responses, for example decision-contingent biases in estimates like anchoring (Spicer et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2024).

text.text: More generally, DDMs do not fully specify the processes supporting choice, offering an abstracted vision of evidence accumulation to facilitate RT predictions as opposed to the concrete sampling framework offered by the ABDM.

The breadth of the sampling framework is not just across responses within decision making, but also across tasks: while we have focused here on extending the ABS to value-based choice, the model retains its prior applications to other domains, continuing to predict a number of empirical phenomena in estimation (e.g., anchoring, repulsion), probability judgments (e.g., conservatism, unpacking effects), response times (e.g., speed-accuracy trade-offs, slow vs. fast errors) and confidence (e.g., metacognitive inefficiency), as originally outlined in Zhu et al. (2024).

text.text: This reinforces that the definition of the ABDM given here is an extension of the existing framework to a new domain rather than an entirely new model, linking choice processes to a common sampling system used across a range of tasks.

This then opens the possibility of examining the performance of this framework across these domains, for example fitting the model to a perceptual task and then using this fit to predict behaviour in preferential decision making (e.g., Frydman and Nave, 2017).

text.text: Moreover, the generality of sampling itself allows for further applications to new domains by simply switching out the target distribution according to the task at hand: distributions could reflect perceptual features, semantic memory, or linguistic space, with the same sampling algorithm being used to access these distributions to support varying responses.
This particular aspect of the sampling framework is a further distinction from the more focused decision making models which are not intended to be applied outside of choice contexts.

We should note that the definition of the ABDM presented here is not the only method to adapt this sampling framework to value-based choices, as previous models have offered differing answers to both what is sampled and accumulated: for example, 'Decision by Sampling' suggests that samples are not limited to potential outcomes from the presented options but also draw from the decision maker's memory of all experienced values (Stewart et al., 2006), while DFT accumulates differences in outcomes between options rather than the wins and losses used here (Bhatia, 2014; Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993).

There are however some limitations of the present study which should be noted.

First, while we evaluate the candidate models in multiple response modalities, we do not perform any joint fitting across these response types, with RTs and confidence judgments instead being inferred from fits to choice.

Such joint fitting can prove challenging to ensure fit metrics over differing datasets are evenly weighted, but could provide greater assurance that the ABDM truly offers the better explanation across measures.

As previously referenced, however, this approach does offer a form of generalisation test (Busemeyer & Wang, 2000), and so could in fact be seen as a strength of this study: the ABDM demonstrates high accuracy in predicted RTs even when its parameters are fit to other data (though from the same task), providing some assurance that this is not simply the result of overfitting.

text.text: Fits are also limited by the number of simulations used to evaluate the models: we restricted comparisons to 100 parameter sets per model for tractability, but this may not be sufficient to fully cover the relatively large parameter space of the ABDM.
More extensive simulations are thus advisable to verify the robustness of these results, though these will naturally carry greater computational costs.
The current comparisons are also entirely focused on risky choice, potentially limiting the generality of our conclusions.

Risky choice is a dominant paradigm within decision making research, and has provided the basis for many key models, including those considered here (Bhatia, 2014; Birnbaum, 2008; Erev et al., 2017; Glöckner & Pachur, 2012; Kellen et al., 2020; Rieskamp, 2008; Tversky & Kahneman, 1992), but extensions to other forms of choice will provide valuable tests of the true breadth of the ABDM.

text.text: The generality of the sampling framework should allow application to other forms of choice, though further minor adjustments to the model to suit these tasks may be required.

Even within this paradigm, we have focused on a particular task design from Erev et al. (2017) and Plonsky et al. (2025) in which choices are directly repeated multiple times, which may not offer a fair reflection of wider choice behaviour.

(2025)</ref> in which choices are directly repeated multiple times, which may not offer a fair reflection of wider choice behaviour.

text.text: This particularly applies to the RT analyses: such repetition leads to particular patterns in choice timing, with much slower RTs in the first instance of each decision.

This could lead to suggestions that the advantage of the ABDM in these results is specific to this task; indeed, a supplementary analysis found model performance was more even if only considering the first trial (see Appendix E).
At the same time, our results show that these tasks offer a method to distinguish these models based on their account for repeated choice, illustrating the value of this design.

Relatedly, while the current model does account for feedback, it does not capture decisions made from experience alone, which will require further adjustments to the definition of the sampling space in the absence of objective descriptions.
Similar criticisms do however also apply to the other candidate models which also lack concrete predictions when nothing is initially known about the choice options.

Finally, these comparisons also consider only a subset of the many choice models from the existing literature: the current candidates were specifically chosen given their prevalence in past research, reflecting key theories for comparison with our approach, but are certainly not exhaustive given the number of models available in this area.
Further contrasts with such candidates will thus help place the ABDM within the wider space of decision making theories.
We have presented the Autocorrelated Bayesian Decision Maker, a new application of mental sampling to value-based choice further expanding the scope of this already broad framework to this domain.

Our results show that this model offers a wider coverage of choice behaviour than many existing theories, accurately describing human choices and response times in both absolute and relative terms, as well as key effects in choice confidence.
This represents a broader perspective on human decision making not only capturing a wider array of behaviours within these tasks but also linking theories of decision making to other domains.

These results then support the suggestion that part of the ABDM's advantage in the main analysis is due to the structure of the considered tasks: when the competing models are not required to balance fitting both the slower initial trials and faster later trials, model performance becomes more even.

This does however demonstrate a key difference in the assumptions of these models, revealing a method to discriminate their predictions: assuming a consistent decision process across repeated choices is clearly insufficient to capture the timing patterns of actual behaviour.
We thus retain focus on the RT analyses considering all trials in the main text as we argue this offers a more stringent test of model behaviour.
